January 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 3
Thank you to those members that come out to “the
hall” to setup and then stay behind to put things
away. We are a volunteer organization and as an
old saying goes “many hands make for small work”.
Twenty Twenty-Four should be the year that every
member puts something more into the Guild than
just their dues.
Where do we need people to help out? To start,
our stalwart Audio-Visual team would like some
breathing room and would really appreciate a few
people to come on board to learn the system. Despite the growing pains as we transitioned
into the hybrid format, from what I have seen close
up, once you are familiar with “the buttons” it is
pretty easy to run. And our A-V team of Shawn,
Matt, and Brian are really friendly.
On the topic of volunteering, next month is elections. There is basically just one qualification to be
on the Board and that is energy. Proficiency at turning is not a prerequisite. The positions that are
open for nominations are: President, Secretary, and
3 Member at Large. If you would like to put your
name forward please let me or anyone else on the
Board know.
Thank you to Steve Daechsel & Bill Fowle for
providing last meeting’s demonstrations. My biggest takeaway from Steve is to put safety first while
in and around the shop. Bill showed us how to handle CA as a finish using oil as a lubricant – I would
never have guessed that!
Speaking of demos, we are seeking someone to
take over from Sheila as our Program Coordinator –
this is the role that finds demonstrators for our
monthly Guild night. This role needs someone with
a general knowledge of wood turning and mostly
seeks demonstrators from within our talented
group (Yes, we all have a talent!). Again, proficiency
at turning is not required to be the Coordinator.
As a Guild we are currently seeking to bring in top
turners/teachers in order to resume Saturday allday demos with follow-up classes. It has been a
long time coming and now that the world has returned to normalcy we can look forward to making
this happen.
The President’s Challenge for February is “turning
air”. You can think in terms of natural edge, voids,
negative space, or maybe you have a different interpretation?
Steve

to see more! Would love to see content from first

January 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 4
Health and safety are top of mind for most wood
workers. We follow many if not all of the best
safety practices highlighted in the 2023 October
issue of the Greater Vancouver Woodturning
Guild’s newsletter (Working Alone in the Shop).
This compilation of practices and advice touched
on the importance of having a first aid kit in our
workshops, leaving us to ask what should be in a
first aid kit? That question was put to a few west
coast turners with working experiences with first
aid kits. Here’s what they had to say.
First Aid Kit Options
Many of us have basic generic first aid kits around
the house or in our shops. Oddly enough some of
us do not know what’s in them or oftentimes are
unable to find what we need in a time of crisis.
Generally, they are of limited value. However, if
you like the idea of owning a commercial kit do
your homework and see what’s available to suit
your needs. Wood working groups may find it prudent to stock a store-bought kit from a due diligence standpoint; assuming members are on site
who know how to use it properly. St John’s Ambulance sells a variety of kits ranging in price from
$20 to $200. Most reputable tool and safety
equipment suppliers sell kits.
Homemade kits:
For most of us, a basic first aid kit is one that we
can make ourself for under $50. The advantage of
this approach is that you will know exactly what it
contains and have an inkling of the expiry date of
its contents. Choose a kit container that is accessible in an emergency, airtight (to keep out moisture, germs and dust), durable and easy to open.
A snap down food container or a repurposed first
aid kit pouch are options to consider. If you stop
heating your shop in winter months you may want
to relocate the kit to a warm location.
Kit content suggestions:
Bandages: Bandages are the mainstay of every
basic first aid kit. Stock a variety of shapes and sizes. Sizes as big as 1 ¾ by 4 inches are sometimes
called for. Consider buying brand names as they
tend to last longer - watch out for sales in your local drugstore. If you are prone to finger injuries
consider buying four-pronged (knuckle) bandages
as they handle hard to cover areas and adhere
well. You may have to go online to get these. If
you like buying in bulk and anticipate a high turnover of stock check out the bandage kits at Costco.
Think about sharing bandages and other duplicate
supplies with fellow wood workers.
Pressure bandages: These are intended for serious
bleeds and most likely need to be purchased on
line. Canadian Safety Supplies carries a First Aid
Central brand worth considering. The 4 in. by 6.5
(Continued on page 5)

January 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 5
in. compression bandage comes with elastic ties
that eliminate the need for pins or tape to hold it in
place. Military grade compression bandages consisting of a dressing pad and a self-applied wrap
can also be purchased on line. As an alternative,
consider purchasing a package of panty linersavailable in small quantities in your drugstore.
They come in different thicknesses (scent free and
wingless are best) and are sealed individually. Use
an ample amount of tape or elastic roll to keep
pressure bandages firmly against the wound.
The most serious of injuries, those involving arterial bleeding, call for the application of direct pressure (with fingers or a pressure bandage) on the
artery leading to the injury to stop the bleeding.
This is where having had first aid instruction covering pressure points on arteries pays dividends.
Once a serious hand bleed injury is under control
try to keep your hand elevated above your head as
high as you can until help is reached. Your body
will attempt to slow the flow of blood to wounded
elevated extremities.
Gauze and adhesive tape: Gauze is available in
rolls and pads. Gauze and tape, along with elastic
bandage wrap rolls with clips are generally useful
for a variety of tasks. Some of the wraps now
come with Velcro fasteners.
Scissors and tweezers: You may be able to sequester these items from old kits or from the medicine cabinet (with Significant Other approval). A
utility knife blade or scalpel blade (taped at one
end) makes for a useful cutting edge.
Hydrogen peroxide: Peroxide may be useful to
flush a minor wound before applying a bandage. It
comes in small bottles. Keep in mind that the priority in a serious accident is to stop the bleeding and
get help as quickly as possible. A serious wound
can be cleaned later by a health professional.
Eye drops: A 30 ml container of Clear Eyes or other
sterile eye liquid would be useful to flush your eye
to remove particles or relieve distress. Do not rub
an injured eye. Any and all eye injuries must be
promptly addressed by professionals.
Ointments: Ointments with antibiotics such as
Polysporin may be useful for those small scrapes,
cuts and burns that are slow to heal. Ointments
treat infection and help speed healing.
Tourniquet: The consensus here is that the use of
a tourniquet is best left
to those trained in its
proper use. Improper
use may cause more
damage
than
good.
Once you are comfortable using one, a Turnkey
Tourniquet
is
recommended. They are inexpensive and can be purchased online.
Cell telephone: Okay, no one keeps a cell phone in
a first aid kit. However, you should always have
one on you while plying your craft. If you become
seriously injured and/or restricted in movement
you will need to call for help immediately. You
don’t want trying to get to a phone somewhere
else to be your last move.
Further enlightenment
Wood working groups would be well served to host
a First Aid training course for their members.
Many clubs have assigned safety officers for working events and presumably taken the time to itemize their responsibilities. Wouldn’t it be wonderful
if we could share those responsibilities with other
clubs, along with this list or a modification of it?
Special thanks to Al Lundgren who did much of the
heavy lifting in developing this piece. Ed Pretty and
several members of the Comox Valley Woodturners
Society also offered valuable input. - Ted Muir

January 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 6
“I once ran my finger into a big grinder at the WFI
Gordon River Shop at 10:00 PM on a Saturday
evening, in the dark of winter. No one else was
there.
I unlatched the metal first aid kit that was mounted
on a post then stared hopelessly at all the sealed
little boxes ... with no identity!
By the process of elimination, I handled many packages until I found, what was likely, a box of 'supersize' band-aids.
I tried with my good hand and fingers to rupture
the plastic that encased the box. I held the box
with three fingers while I tried to find a weak point
with my other two fingers. This meant I had to
discontinue the 'applied pressure of survival' with
which my good hand had been tasked.
While I fumbled and probed this sealed unit with
my perfectly fine hand, the blood from my wound
gushed and dripped upon the shop floor adding to
the 'blood spatter trail' from the grinder, 20 feet
away, creating an even larger pool at my feet.
The next attempt was with my teeth since I had
chosen,
once again, to apply pressure with my shirt and
good hand. My teeth were not the tools I required.
Momentarily I thought about using the very same
grinder that had harmed me as it was still whirring
and shaking on the shop floor but no....I had a
better plan.
Frustration, anger and some fear propelled me to
the blacksmith shop, 50 feet away, in the opposite
direction. I dropped the little tightly wrapped box
on the anvil, after I picked it up from where it had
bounced onto the dirt floor.
With a bit more patience and focus, the little box
was now where I wanted it. From the rack, next to
the forge, I seized the biggest hammer I believed I
could heft with one arm.
My plan was to carefully smack the very end of this
damn box which might, using physics and perhaps
a bit of chemistry from the heat generated on impact, rupture the tough plastic prophylactic that
kept me from administering my first aid.
The 'full on blow' was poorly aimed and although
the box finally released its contents of 'Q-Tips' I
was not making progress.
Two more cycles to and from the metal first aid
box resulted in various emergency product packages and contents strewn upon the floor around the
anvil before I 'hit' the jackpot; a glancing blow that
sheared the end of a box that contained undamaged band-aids.”
The following article is reprinted with the kind
permission of Al Lundgren. Al Lundgren is a major
player in initiating safety guidelines in the timber
industry at large. For more information about Al
and his role as a health and safety pioneer, check
out this YouTube video by WorkSafeBC.

January 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 7
December…and the start of January…it’s been
harsh, full of chaos, blessings, and not much actual
woodturning. As my woodturning journey continues, I am coming to appreciate that events, whether monumental or mundane, need to be taken in
stride and all the plans for making and getting to
the lathe simply stop and one gets swept up in the
other priorities that come along.
And while I rarely got to put tools to use, I did manage to apply my skills and knowledge gained on
this woodturning adventure to good use.
For example…I fixed my toilet. My brother-in-law
helped me diagnose the issue and recommended a
course of action for me to apply. Parts picked up,
bucket and tools in hand, I went to work on completing the repair. I almost got hung up on the fact
that I could not get the new nut onto the hose
when I remembered all those discussions about TPI
and threading to realize they were the same
thread, and I could easily using the old one that
was already in place. KISS! It got done! I felt empowered and the simple act of having a toilet that
no longer hissed through the night was taken as a
win.
Other wins happened too. Remember how I mentioned I did a class with Elizabeth Weber? Well
online, she was connected to another new turner
who is breaking into the market of becoming a demonstrator, one bowl at a time. Tina from
@woodturnter was coming to Vancouver and connecting with Natasha…a brand-new turner who
lives in Surrey, BC. I had Tina come by for a sit/visit
in my shop, which first had to be cleared of the
hordes of wood that I had recently gathered thanks
to the generosity and connections of so many in
our guild. For those who know the state of my
shop, that was no small feat. But wow, the space
was so appreciated and continues as the stash got
squirrelled away into other spaces until the spring.
Tina helped make the connection of why bowls
begin as they typically do for new turners with a
shape that is square and has a flat bottom. She
also has a nifty set of visuals she made of how to
get the transformation into a shape one may find
more pleasing, even comparing the shapes of
bowls one makes when one takes classes from
makers like Glenn Lucas, Kirk DeHeer, and Mike
Mahoney, to name but a few. She has been so
lucky to travel and have taken classes with these
turners, so her skills have developed in a short
time. She is going to the AAW Symposium in Portland so I’m looking forward to reconnecting with
her there.
Tasha and I also connected, and she is at
the very beginning of
her journey…where I
was a few years ago. It
was fantastic to show
and share a bunch of
things I have learned
along the way and to
spark
and
fan
the
flames of her foray into
woodturning. I think
we have much in common and it once again allowed me to appreciate how far I have come with
the help of so many.
And I must mention the absolute epic day of
getting to give a go at hollowing with the assistance
and direction of Phil Winch and Dan Breck. I am
one step closer to making the vision happen and
was so emboldened and thrilled with the next
steps…until life interrupted. But that project is still
there for me to percolate and consider the possibility of what comes next. But seeing the video of
that wide grin on my face, fully engaged, and doing
something I thought I would never ever consider
doing. And is it possible that a chainsaw just might
be in my future? I so want a bigger lathe…but unfortunately, the new shop with a cement floor
would have to come first…and that is unlikely to
(Continued on page 8)

January 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 8
happen soon. So much
for the decision in 2002
that said we could live
without a garage as we
considered our 80/20
when buying our first
house!
So, I will take every opportunity to I can to
connect and turn with
others.
While
woodturning is often
described as a lonely
craft with just you, your chunk, the tools, and the
lathe, I have also managed to tap into a wonderful
network of others who also enjoy the experience,
and even like to connect, socialize, and share with
others too. It also brought me tremendous joy to
receive a text message from Dan Breck’s daughter
asking for the details of the tool we used to remove a bunch of wood from that chunk of cherry
before we went to Phil’s place. The Strongbore
Extension from Lee Valley, which I learned about
during one of the Monday
night Tech Talks that I was
able to attend before scheduling conflicts came to be. I
really miss those as I’ve noticed it has been a way to
practice listening to random
comments that could then be
added to my toolkit and
pulled out another day and
way…like when fixing toilets.
I am also super appreciative of the energy and
effort Diana has been doing to tap and encourage
members to share a little bit about themselves,
their woodturning and other pursuits that have
made them who they are in the Guild Member profile in this newsletter. This month we will be treated by a profile on Dan Moleschi. It has been delightful getting to know Dan better as we took the
Elizabeth Weber class together and we have now
spent time in his shop exploring making pens with
plan to do some glue ups of blanks. I am in complete awe of how organized his shop is…and chuckle when he mentions he was organizing it more.
He has provided with a vision of a gold standard
that I so desperately want to strive towards.
Meanwhile, we have plans to play. And he is an
absolutely avid gardener, so I am looking forward
to tapping into that wealth of experience and
knowledge too. Might it be possible for keeping
my orchids alive and thriving this coming year?
So, despite all my projects having to sit a bit and
wait for my capacity to turn to return, I am so thoroughly grateful for the connections and shared experiences and knowledge. It is so very upsetting
and disappointing that I have had to pull back from
taking on the coordinating role for our monthly
meetings, appreciating just how important a role
this is, and that on my own, I simply am not able to
do the task, but I am thrilled that Paul Russell from
Utah has been lined up to do this months IRD for
the Guild’s January meeting. But like my many projects, the ideas and seeds will sit and store, perhaps germinating for the moment when capacity
returns, life commitments settle, and I will be able
to burst forth to do the things that I absolutely
ache and crave to do.
Until then, I will appreciate that both Grandad
(Mike’s dad) and my mom are out of the hospital.
Really…the health care workers…all of them…
deserve our utter appreciation, respect for doing
what they do. We really do need to pay them
more! Meanwhile, I will work towards that gold
standard of creating space and organizing myself,
so we are better able to handle dealing with bedbugs and confused beetles that entered our home.
I will continue to make the most of each experience I get to advance the love of making, either on
my own, or with others. Oh…and I will get a group
order organized for pen supplies. There are a few
of us that are super keen to get supplies from William Wood-Write so here may be an opportunity to
get a group discount and share the shipping. Until
then, I did get a bunch more supplies from KMS to
keep the pen adventure thriving. Look for the details still to come.

January 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 9
Tell us about your background - how did you
get into woodturning?
When I turned 50 years old, I asked myself, if I was
to pass tomorrow, what would I regret not doing in
my life. I answered “work with wood”. I knew I
wouldn’t have the patience for a lengthy project. I
remembered my grandfather's shop and in it was a
lathe. I thought a lathe project should be much
quicker to complete.
In 2007 I bought a used Nova 3000 DVR and pieced
together some lathe tools. I joined the GVWG in
2012 and FVWG in 2017.
I started my education in turning by taking 101
classes with the guild and going to see the demonstrators that the turning clubs brought in. Then I
volunteered to assist in classes organized by Jerry
Vickers, Barry Wilkinson, Peter Hill and Jay Mapson.
Currently I have done pen turning demonstrations
at KMS Coquitlam and Abbotsford and woodturning demonstrations at Langley Arts Alive.
My work generally goes to family and friends as
gifts. I have donated my work to charities to be
entered into silent auctions.
Tell us about your workshop/studio
My Shop is a 400 sq.ft. room, separated from my 2
car garage. The room is below ground level so it
remains cool in summer and comfortable in winter.
(Continued on page 10)

January 2024
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page 10
The shop contains:
•
2 hp dust collector
•
Suspended air cleaner
•
2hp table saw - General
•
Sliding compound miter saw - Makita
•
15" Bandsaw Hammer N3800
•
20" Powermatic lathe
I like the size of my
lathe and the headstock
slides
the
length of the bed so I
can work standing at
the end of the bed to
work on the inside of
the bowl.
Some of the projects I
do are: bowls, peppermills, pens, tealight
holders
and
Christmas ornaments.
What finishes do you prefer using?
I have had greatest success using A & B Wood
Bleach on Maple burl Christmas ornaments, then
lacquer spray and buffing for the final result.
My go-to finish on bowls is multiple coats of wipeon poly.
Pens - I color the turned pen blanks then apply a
CA finish then polish the pen.
What is your favourite wood?
I like wood when you find the beauty where it is
not expected. I guess my favourite wood is the
wood I haven’t turned before.
Are there any new techniques you would like
to try?
I want to explore texturing and coloring in my
work. I have done limited hollowing and would like
to get more involved with that.
I consider there are 3 types of turners:
•
Functional Turners - incorporating turning into
furniture, Architectural (buildings)
•
Crafter - Making everyday objects you recognize but with a flare
•
Artistic Turners - Where turnings become art
•
OR - a combination of any of the above.
I consider myself a Crafter.
Favourite sayings - “if you think it’s good enough its
not” and "Turn it up a notch"
Who has been the greatest influence on your
work?
My inspiration comes from abroad and local, - -
Some of my favorites are Jimmy Clewes, Glen Lucas, Cindy Drozda and John Spitters.

I put this bowl together at my brother in-law
Bruce's shop in upstate New York. Bruce had
worked out the layout and helped me with each
step. After doing all the steps, I did not have time
to turn it before coming home. I brought the bowl
back, not yet turned. It took me a while to get it
back on the lathe and turn it. It was a different
challenge putting it on a different chuck and that
made me somewhat nervous. It was harder to turn
than I was thought and a good learning experience
over all. I was happy with it, of course now I know
what I might do differently. I used a table saw Jig to
cut each piece and held each layer together with
round stainless steel pipe clamp before gluing each
layer together. An appropriate size clamps for
each layer. Glued it up with Titebond wood glue.
Each layer was glued on piece the lathe.

15% Discount for GVWG Members!
How to Qualify:
•
Stop giving your phone number at the cashier
counter. (Will be hard because we have been
doing this for years).
•
Only tell them you are with the GVWG or
Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild.
•
Either statement will link your purchase to your
new 15% discount.
If you give the cashier your phone number, you
will only get the store 5% non-guild price.
By saying GVWG instead you get 15% guild price
If you are buying something that needs a warranty,
you just give them your Name and Address and
that will go on the electronic file.
If the item you are buying has a flyer sale that is
better than the 15%, then you will automatically
get the better price.
Every purchase you make in the store by doing the
above process adds to our GVWG Credit account.
We use this credit account to buy KMS Gift certificate prizes and even bought our Laguna lathe for
Sapperton Hall with this credit account. By doing
this you are giving yourself a better discount and
helping the guild at the same time.
If you are an out of town guild member, all you
have to do is type in GVWG as the customer name
when buying, and type in your full name, address
etc. in the ship to and you will get the 15% discount.
The 15% is an average savings and is based on the
cost margins from that manufacturer. This does
not apply to published special flyer items.
If we all do this, we can even get up to a bigger discount level in future!

 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock

with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage.
